title: Writing a Short Story
bigQuestion: What makes a short story in Spanish easy for a reader to follow from beginning to end?

story.title: The Red Backpack Comes Home
story.kicker: Marco loses his red backpack on the bus, and a kind stranger helps it find its way back.
paragraphs: Marco has a red backpack. In Spanish he calls it la mochila roja (the red backpack). It holds his books, his pencils and a photo of his dog. On Monday, Marco rides the bus to school with his sister, Elena.

Marco is sleepy. He puts the backpack on the seat. The bus stops at the school, and Marco jumps off fast. Then he stops. "¡Mi mochila!" (My backpack!) The backpack is still on the bus. The bus is already gone.

Marco feels sad. "Estoy triste," he says. (I am sad.) Elena says, "Vamos a la oficina." (Let's go to the office.) The secretary calls the bus company. "Una mochila roja, pero pequeña," Marco says. (A red backpack, but small.)

On the bus, a woman sees the backpack. She opens the front pocket. She finds a card with Marco's name and school. She gives the backpack to the driver. The driver brings it back to the school in the afternoon.

At three o'clock, the secretary calls Marco. There it is: la mochila roja. Everything is inside, and the photo of his dog too. Marco smiles. "¡Gracias!" Now he tells the story in order: a beginning, a middle and a happy end.
story.think: What is the beginning, the middle and the end of Marco's story? Say each part in one short sentence.

lessons.title: Joining with Y
lessons.mainIdea: Y means and; it joins two words or two short sentences into one.
reading: Picture two short sentences: "Como arroz." "Como frijoles." They sound choppy. Join them with y (and): "Como arroz y frijoles." (I eat rice and beans.) Now it is one smooth sentence.
Y can join two actions too. "Leo un libro y juego con mi perro." (I read a book and I play with my dog.) Y is one letter, and it is said like the ee in see. It does not need a comma before it.
A common mistake is to repeat y too much: "Como y leo y juego y duermo." Use commas for a list: "Como, leo, juego y duermo." Put y only before the last item, the same way English uses and.

words.d: and — joins words or ideas: Como arroz y frijoles (I eat rice and beans)
the sentence — a whole thought with someone and an action

look.title: Two Become One
look.text: Marco writes: "Tengo una mochila. Tengo un perro." (I have a backpack. I have a dog.) He joins them: "Tengo una mochila y un perro." (I have a backpack and a dog.) The sentence is shorter and smoother.
look.prompt: Join these two sentences with y: Leo un libro. Como una manzana.

check.why: Y means and. It joins two words or ideas.
Use commas in a list and put y only before the last item.

check.q: What does "Leo un libro y juego" mean?
choices: I read a book and I play.
I read a book but I play.
check.why: Leo means I read, y means and, and juego means I play.

lessons.title: Changing Direction with Pero
lessons.mainIdea: Pero means but; it joins two ideas that go in different directions.
reading: Picture this: Marco loves the bus, but he is sleepy. The second idea surprises us. In Spanish, *pero* (but) joins ideas like that. "Me gusta el bus, pero estoy cansado." (I like the bus, but I am tired.)

Put a comma before pero, just like before but in English. "La mochila es roja, pero es pequeña." (The backpack is red, but it is small.) Pero tells the reader: get ready, something different is coming.
Do not mix up pero and perro. Pero with one r means but. Perro with rr means dog. Say them out loud. The rr in perro is rolled. A missing r changes the meaning of your whole sentence.

words.d: but — joins two ideas that differ: Me gusta leer, pero no me gusta correr
the dog — spelled with rr; do not mix it up with pero (but)

look.title: A Surprise in the Middle
look.text: Elena writes: "Voy a la escuela. No tengo mi mochila." Those two ideas do not match, so she joins them with pero: "Voy a la escuela, pero no tengo mi mochila." (I go to school, but I do not have my backpack.)
look.prompt: Finish this sentence with pero: Me gusta la pizza, pero…

check.why: Pero with one r means but. Perro with rr means dog.

choices: Me gusta el sol, pero hace calor.
check.why: Pero joins two ideas that differ: I like the sun, but it is hot.

check.q: What does "La mochila es roja, pero es pequeña" mean?
choices: The backpack is red and big.
The dog is red and small.
The backpack is red, but it is small.
check.why: Roja is red, pero is but, and pequeña is small.

lessons.title: Adding More with También
lessons.mainIdea: También means also or too; it adds one more matching idea.
reading: Picture Elena and Marco at lunch. Marco says, "Como arroz." Elena says, "Yo *también*." (Me too.) También means also or too. It adds something that matches what came before.

You can put también after the verb: "Leo un libro. Leo una revista también." Or before the verb: "También leo una revista." (I also read a magazine.) Both are correct. Notice the accent on the last syllable: tam-BIÉN.
A common mistake is using también to show a difference. That is the job of pero. También is for more of the same kind. "Juego fútbol. También juego béisbol." Both ideas are sports, so they match.

words.d: also, too — adds a matching idea: Yo también (Me too)
Me too — a quick way to agree with someone

look.title: Me Too at Lunch
look.text: Marco: "Me gusta el arroz." (I like rice.) Elena: "A mí también." (Me too.) Marco: "Juego fútbol después." (I play soccer afterward.) Elena: "Yo también juego." (I play too.) Each también adds a matching idea.
look.prompt: Tell one thing you do, then add a second matching thing with también.

check.why: También means also or too and adds a matching idea.
También has an m before the b and an accent on the last e.

check.q: Pick the best word: "Leo libros. ___ leo cómics."
check.why: Reading comics matches reading books, so también (also) fits.

lessons.title: Beginning, Middle and End
lessons.mainIdea: A good short story has a beginning that sets the scene, a middle with a problem and an end.
reading: Think of Marco's story. At the beginning, we meet Marco and his red backpack. In the middle, there is a problem: the backpack stays on the bus. At the end, the problem is solved and he gets it back.

In Spanish, these parts are *el principio* (the beginning), el medio (the middle) and *el final* (the end). The beginning tells who and where. The middle tells what goes wrong. The end tells how it turns out.
Order words help. Start the beginning with primero. Use luego or después in the middle. Start the end with finalmente. A reader who sees finalmente knows the story is closing.

words.d: the beginning — tells who is in the story and where
the end — tells how the problem turns out
the problem — what goes wrong in the middle; a masculine word even though it ends in -a

look.title: Three Parts of Marco's Story
look.text: Principio: "Marco tiene una mochila roja." (Marco has a red backpack.) Medio: "Después, la mochila está en el bus." (After that, the backpack is on the bus.) Final: "Finalmente, Marco tiene su mochila." (Finally, Marco has his backpack.)
look.prompt: Tell a tiny story about a lost toy in three sentences: a beginning, a middle and an end.

check.q: Which part of a story tells what goes wrong?
check.why: The middle has the problem. The end tells how it turns out.
El final is the end of the story.

check.q: Which sentence is best for the end of Marco's story?
choices: La mochila está en el bus.
check.why: Finalmente signals the end, and the problem is solved.

lessons.title: Four to Six Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: A short story in Spanish can be four to six sentences, each one a clear step.
reading: Picture a story as a set of stairs. Each sentence is one step. Four to six steps are enough for a short story. Too few steps, and the reader misses something. Too many, and the reader gets lost.

Here is a six-sentence story. "Es sábado. Primero, voy al parque. Luego, juego con mi perro. Pero mi perro corre. Después, busco a mi perro. Finalmente, está en casa." Each sentence moves the story forward.
Keep each sentence short and complete. Each one needs someone and an action. "Mi perro corre" (My dog runs) is complete. "Mi perro grande" (My big dog) is not a sentence. It has no action.

words.d: the story, short tale — Escribo un cuento (I write a story)
to write — escribo means I write

look.title: Counting the Steps
look.text: "Es lunes. Primero, voy a la escuela. Luego, leo un cuento. Pero no tengo mi lápiz. Después, mi amiga me da un lápiz. Finalmente, escribo mi cuento." Count the sentences. There are six. Find the problem: no tengo mi lápiz (I do not have my pencil).
look.prompt: Write a four-sentence story about a day at the park. Use at least two order words.

check.q: How many sentences does a short story in this lesson need?
check.why: Four to six clear sentences are enough for a short story.

check.q: Which one is a complete sentence?
check.why: Mi perro corre has someone (my dog) and an action (runs).
Escribo means I write, and un cuento is a story.

lessons.title: A Comic Strip in Spanish
lessons.mainIdea: A comic strip tells a story in boxes; each box can hold one short Spanish sentence.
reading: Picture a comic strip with four boxes. Each box is one step. In Spanish, a comic strip is often called *la historieta*. Each box is a panel, called la viñeta. The words people say go in a speech bubble.
Box 1: Marco on the bus. "Tengo sueño." (I am sleepy.) Box 2: the school. "¡Mi mochila!" Box 3: the office. "Estoy triste." Box 4: the backpack returns. "¡Gracias!" Four boxes tell a whole story.
Keep bubble words short. Use ¡ and ! for exclaiming, and ¿ and ? for asking. The upside-down mark goes at the start. A common mistake is to write only the end mark, like in English.

words.d: the comic strip — a story told in boxes with pictures
the panel — one box of a comic strip

look.title: Four Boxes
look.text: Box 1: a girl sees rain. "¡Llueve!" (It is raining!) Box 2: she looks for her umbrella. "¿Dónde está mi paraguas?" (Where is my umbrella?) Box 3: her dog has it. Box 4: she laughs. "¡Gracias, perro!"
look.prompt: Plan a four-box comic about your morning. Write one short Spanish sentence for each box.

check.why: La historieta is a comic strip, a story told in boxes.
Spanish exclamations open with ¡ and close with !.

check.q: What is one box of a comic strip called?
check.why: La viñeta is one panel, or box, of a comic strip.

lessons.title: Check Every Verb Ending
lessons.mainIdea: The verb ending must match who does the action: -o for yo, -as or -es for tú, -a or -e for él and ella.
reading: You finished your story. Now check it like a detective. Look at every verb. Ask: who does this? If it is you, the ending is usually -o: *hablo*, como, escribo. If it is Marco, it is usually -a or -e: habla, come, escribe.
Here is a sentence with a mistake: "Marco como arroz." Who eats? Marco, not me. So the verb must be come: "Marco come arroz." (Marco eats rice.) The -o ending only works for yo.
English speakers make this mistake because English verbs barely change: I eat, he eats. In Spanish, the ending carries the meaning. Check each verb, one by one, before you share your story.

words.d: I speak — from hablar; the -o ending means yo
he or she speaks — from hablar; the -a ending means él or ella

look.title: Detective Check
look.text: Elena reads Marco's story: "Mi hermana camino a la escuela." She asks, "Who walks?" Mi hermana (my sister) is ella. So camino is wrong. The fix: "Mi hermana camina a la escuela." (My sister walks to school.)
look.prompt: Fix this sentence: Marco juego con su perro.

check.why: Marco is él, so comer becomes come.
In the present tense, most yo forms end in -o: hablo, como, escribo.

choices: Mi hermana camina a la escuela.
Mi hermana camino a la escuela.
Mi hermana caminar a la escuela.
Mi hermana caminas a la escuela.
check.why: Mi hermana is ella, so caminar becomes camina.

lessons.title: Check Nouns and Describing Words
lessons.mainIdea: A describing word matches its noun: la mochila roja, el libro rojo, los libros rojos.
reading: Look again at Marco's backpack: la mochila roja. Mochila is feminine, so the describing word ends in -a: roja. A book is masculine: el libro rojo. The describing word changes to match the noun.

Plural nouns need plural describing words. "Los libros rojos" (the red books). "Las mochilas rojas" (the red backpacks). Add -s to both. In Spanish, the describing word usually comes after the noun, not before like in English.

Common mistakes: "la mochila rojo" (wrong ending) and "la roja mochila" (English order). Some describing words end in -e, like *grande* (big). They stay the same for both: el perro grande, la casa grande.

words.d: red — rojo, roja, rojos, rojas to match the noun: la mochila roja
big — the same for masculine and feminine: el perro grande, la casa grande

look.title: Match It Up
look.text: el libro rojo (the red book) → la mochila roja (the red backpack) → los libros rojos (the red books) → las mochilas rojas (the red backpacks). Look at the last letters. The noun and the describing word end the same way.
look.prompt: Describe your own backpack or bag in Spanish. Check that the endings match.

check.q: Which is correct for "the red backpack"?
check.why: Mochila is feminine, so it takes la and roja, and the describing word goes after the noun.

check.q: Which is correct for "the big dogs"?
check.why: Perros is plural, so grande becomes grandes, and los matches too.

check.q: Which describing word stays the same for el and la?
check.why: Words ending in -e, like grande, are the same for masculine and feminine.

lessons.title: Read It Aloud
lessons.mainIdea: Reading your story aloud helps you hear missing words, wrong endings and choppy sentences.
reading: Picture yourself reading your story to a friend. Your ears catch things your eyes miss. If a sentence sounds strange, stop and check it. Maybe a word is missing, or an ending is wrong.

Read slowly. Say every vowel clearly: a, e, i, o, u. Spanish vowels have one sound each. Stress the syllable with the accent mark: *después*, también, miércoles. The accent tells your voice where to lean.
Listen for choppy parts. "Como. Leo. Juego." sounds like a robot. Join ideas with y, pero or también. Then ask a friend: "¿Te gusta mi cuento?" (Do you like my story?) Their answer helps you improve.

words.d: to read aloud — Leo mi cuento en voz alta (I read my story aloud)
after that — say it with the stress on the last syllable, where the accent is

look.title: Fixing a Robot Story
look.text: Robot version: "Es domingo. Como. Leo. Juego. Duermo." Better version: "Es domingo. Primero, como y leo. Luego, juego con mi perro. Finalmente, duermo." Same actions, but the order words and y make it flow.
look.prompt: Read your own story aloud. Where can you join two sentences with y, pero or también?

choices: to hear mistakes your eyes missed
check.why: Hearing the story helps you catch missing words and wrong endings.

check.q: In después, which syllable gets the stress?
check.why: The accent mark on é shows the stress: des-PUÉS.

choices: Como y leo y juego y.
Primero, como y leo. Luego, juego.
check.why: Order words and y join the actions into smooth sentences.

review.q: Which word joins two ideas that differ?
review.why: Pero means but and joins ideas that go in different directions.

review.q: Why did Marco lose his backpack in the story?
choices: He left it on the bus.
review.why: Marco was sleepy, jumped off the bus fast and left the backpack on the seat.

review.q: Which is correct for "the small backpacks"?
review.why: Mochilas is feminine plural, so las and pequeñas match it.
Elena is ella, so escribir becomes escribe.

review.q: Which word means also or too?
review.why: También adds a matching idea: also, too.

review.q: Which part of a story tells who and where?
review.why: The beginning, el principio, sets the scene.
Spanish questions open with ¿ and close with ?.

review.q: What does "Como arroz, pero no como frijoles" mean?
choices: I eat rice and also beans.
I do not eat rice or beans.
I eat rice, but I do not eat beans.
review.why: Pero means but, and no before como means I do not eat.
